**(CNN)** — Initially, one might suspect that *Up*, Pixar’s tenth feature-length animated film, is destined to be a rather somber affair. The story centers on Carl, a curmudgeonly widower attempting to navigate the unbridled enthusiasm of a young boy named Russell. While there is certainly no shame in an animated film tugging at the heartstrings, a palpable sense of unease ripples through the younger members of the audience when, just five minutes into a spirited prologue, the intrepid young Carl and Ellie rapidly transition into newlyweds, and eventually into their twilight years. 

We watch them age before our eyes—their youthful dreams of global exploration gradually surrendered to domestic comforts and quiet routines. Ellie longs for a child she cannot have, while their hard-earned savings for a once-in-a-lifetime expedition are repeatedly drained by life’s unpredictable turns and domestic mishaps, until time simply runs out—at least for Ellie. 

This tragic opening leaves us alone with Carl, a taciturn recluse voiced by Ed Asner, whose reticence makes WALL-E seem positively talkative by comparison. Considering he is one of the film's lead characters, it would hardly be surprising if anxious younger viewers were privately wondering when the dancing penguins might arrive. *(Watch a preview of "Up" »)*

Fortunately, such apprehensions are entirely misplaced. When it comes to cinematic spectacle, *Up* delivers in spades. While it offers no dancing penguins, it provides far more than the airborne home promised in the marketing campaign. The journey introduces a fantastical, multicolored bird—possibly a snipe—who answers to the name of Kevin and possesses a keen fondness for chocolate bars. There are majestic zeppelins, legendary explorers, and an entire pack of talking dogs capable of serving wine, playing poker, and piloting biplanes. 

Then, of course, there is Russell: a stout young Boy Scout—or "Wilderness Explorer"—who unexpectedly materializes on Carl’s porch. Desperate for solace, the old man has launched his home into the sky using thousands of helium balloons, entirely unaware that the young boy was standing on his doorstep.

*Up* does not maintain perfection throughout its flight. The slapstick canine antics lean closer to the absurdity of *Beverly Hills Chihuahua* than one typically expects from Pixar, a studio that rarely bends the laws of nature so casually for a quick laugh. Nevertheless, if these chatterbox hounds entertain the younger crowd, so be it. 

The film finds far surer footing as it explores the evolving relationship between Carl and Russell high above the clouds. Russell is a portrait of wide-eyed innocence and relentless, if clumsy, helpfulness—the very mirror image of the boy Carl once was, if only the old man had the clarity to see it. Instead, Carl remains fixated on landing his cherished house atop a prime cliffside location (the mythical Paradise Falls), which he mistakenly views as his ultimate destination. The imagery of Carl valiantly dragging his home across jungles and over mountain peaks will undoubtedly resonate with anyone currently carrying a mortgage. *(iReport.com: Share your review of "Up")*

Written by Bob Peterson and co-directed by Peterson alongside Pete Docter—both seasoned Pixar veterans—*Up* masterfully weaves allegory with high adventure and pure imaginative exuberance. While the thematic balance may not be quite as seamless as in Pixar’s absolute finest works, the film's buoyant spirit is irresistible, anchored by the character of Russell (charmingly voiced by Jordan Nagai). Though carrying his own emotional burdens at just eight years old, Russell is pure heart—the kind of character that gives youth a good name.

Screened in 3D where available, the film wisely avoids superficial stereoscopic gimmicks, instead utilizing depth of field to heighten a series of exhilarating aerial dogfights and cliffhangers. Witty, poignant, and brimming with vitality, *Up* easily stands as one of the finest films of the year so far. It is best experienced with someone you care about.

***Up* is rated PG and has a running time of 96 minutes.** *(For Entertainment Weekly's review, click here.)*

On paper, centering a animated blockbuster around an octogenarian widower dealing with profound grief and the looming threat of being forced into a retirement home seemed like a major commercial risk. Yet, what could have been a relentlessly somber tragedy instead became one of the most beloved masterpieces in modern cinema. Pixar tackled the heavy themes of loss and aging head-on, proving that animated storytelling could engage with deep human melancholy without sacrificing light, joy, and breathtaking wonder.

The emotional bedrock of *Up* is established in its famously devastating opening montage, which chronicles the life of Carl Fredricksen and his soulmate, Ellie. From childhood sweethearts to a happily married couple, their life together is filled with quiet joy, shared dreams, and quiet heartbreaks—most notably their inability to have children and their repeated deferral of a dream trip to Paradise Falls in South America. When Ellie passes away, Carl is left alone in a rapidly modernizing world, trapped in a home heavy with memories and surrounded by noisy construction sites. Facing eviction, Carl makes a radical, defiant decision: he ties thousands of colorful helium balloons to his chimney and floats his entire house into the sky, setting a course for South America to fulfill his late wife’s final wish.

However, Carl’s solitary escape into the clouds is abruptly interrupted by an uninvited stowaway. Russell, an overly enthusiastic, eight-year-old Wilderness Explorer seeking his final merit badge for "Assisting the Elderly," finds himself trapped on Carl’s porch at several thousand feet. Russell’s boundless optimism and desperate need for a father figure stand in stark contrast to Carl’s curmudgeonly, grief-stricken desire to be left alone. This odd-couple dynamic forces Carl to look beyond his own sorrow, setting the stage for a journey of emotional healing.

Once the floating house lands near Paradise Falls, the film deftly shifts gears, alleviating any initial audience fears that the narrative would be a depressing slog. The story bursts into a vibrant, kinetic adventure as Carl and Russell traverse a lush, treacherous jungle. Along the way, they meet a cast of unforgettable characters, including Kevin, a rare, colorful giant bird with a fondness for chocolate, and Dug, an eager Golden Retriever fitted with a translator collar that projects his thoughts into speech. These whimsical elements introduce laugh-out-loud physical comedy and frantic action sequences—such as a dogfight between biplanes piloted by actual canines—that instantly captivate younger audiences.

Underneath the high-flying escapades and talking animals, the film never loses sight of its emotional core. The true triumph of *Up* lies in Carl’s realization that his adventure with Ellie did not end when she died; her grandest endeavor was simply the life they shared together. By letting go of his literal and figurative baggage, Carl opens his heart to a new chapter of connection and mentorship with Russell.

Ultimately, *Up* stands as a masterclass in narrative balance. By fearlessly confronting grief, nostalgia, and mortality, Pixar laid the foundation for a story that resonates profoundly with adults. By surrounding that sadness with bright colors, exhilarating set pieces, and endearing humor, they crafted an accessible, heart-warming treat for children. *Up* proved that family entertainment does not need to shy away from life's heaviest realities to be uplifting; rather, it showed that the brightest adventures are often born from the darkest shadows.

***

### The AI Behind the Magic: How CNNs Are Reshaping Animation for Pixar

For decades, Pixar Animation Studios has stood at the intersection of technological innovation and artistic storytelling. From the groundbreaking release of *Toy Story* in 1995 to the breathtaking, hyper-realistic physics of *Elemental*, Pixar has constantly pushed the boundaries of computer-generated imagery (CGI). Today, a new tool is driving the next evolution in animation: **Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)**.

A **CNN** is a class of deep learning algorithms specially designed to analyze and process visual data. While traditionally used for facial recognition and autonomous driving, these advanced neural networks have found a powerful application in computer graphics. **For** Pixar, the integration of CNN-driven workflows represents a monumental leap in rendering speed, character performance, and visual polish.

#### Accelerated Rendering and Denoising
One of the most computationally expensive steps in modern animation is ray tracing—simulating how light bounces off surfaces to create realistic shadows, reflections, and subsurface scattering. Traditionally, rendering a single frame could take dozens of machine hours. 

To overcome this bottleneck, engineers have deployed **CNNs for** image denoising. By training a neural network on millions of incomplete, "noisy" rendered frames paired with their fully rendered counterparts, the CNN learns to predict what a finished image should look like. Instead of calculating every single photon, Pixar’s render engines can produce a low-sample, noisy frame, and the CNN instantly cleans it up to final picture quality. This saves thousands of hours of computing power, allowing directors to see near-instant previews of complex scenes.

#### Enhancing Physics and Character Details
Creating believable movement **for** complex elements—like Ember’s flowing flames in *Elemental*, Merida’s wild curls in *Brave*, or the realistic folding of clothing—requires dense mathematical simulations. 

CNNs are now being trained on high-fidelity physics simulations. Once trained, the network can predict how cloth, water, or hair should react to a character’s movement in real time. This allows animators to manipulate character models smoothly without waiting for overnight simulation bakes, keeping the creative workflow fluid and intuitive.

#### The Future of Storytelling
Despite the rise of artificial intelligence, Pixar’s core philosophy remains unchanged: technology serves the story, not the other way around. The implementation of deep learning tools like **CNNs for** Pixar isn't about automating creativity or replacing human artists; it is about stripping away tedious, repetitive technical constraints.

By letting machine learning handle the heavy lifting of rendering, noise reduction, and physics approximation, Pixar’s artists are given the freedom to focus on what matters most—crafting unforgettable characters and timeless emotional journeys. The collaboration between human artistry and advanced neural networks ensures that the magic coming out of Pixar will only become more mesmerizing in the years to come.

**LOS ANGELES (CNN)** — Animated films are rarely expected to carry the emotional weight of a heavy live-action drama, but Pixar Animation Studios’ latest release, "Up," flies far past standard family-friendly expectations into the cinematic stratosphere. 

Directed by Pete Docter ("Monsters, Inc."), the film—which opens in theaters nationwide Friday—is a daring, visually spectacular, and surprisingly profound exploration of grief, aging, and the true nature of adventure. 

At a time when Hollywood relies heavily on noisy sequels and high-concept franchises, "Up" stands out as a triumph of original storytelling. It is, quite simply, one of the finest films of the year.

---

### Ten minutes that break your heart

The film introduces audiences to Carl Fredricksen (voiced with brilliant, gruff vulnerability by veteran actor Ed Asner), a 78-year-old retired balloon salesman facing the grim reality of being forced into a retirement home after the passing of his beloved wife, Ellie.

Before the main plot even begins, Docter presents a largely dialogue-free, five-minute montage tracking Carl and Ellie’s life together—from childhood sweethearts to marriage, shared dreams, financial hardships, and ultimately, Ellie’s death. 

It is a masterclass in visual storytelling. The sequence is so unexpectedly powerful that it may leave adults reaching for tissues before their popcorn is even half-eaten. 

"We wanted to capture the beauty of a lifetime love story," Docter told reporters at a recent press screening. "It grounds the rest of the crazy adventure that follows."

### An unlikely crew takes flight

Determined to fulfill a lifelong promise to Ellie to visit South America’s mysterious Paradise Falls, Carl takes extreme measures. Using thousands of helium balloons tied to his chimney, he lifts his entire suburban house into the air, setting sail for the skies.

However, Carl’s quiet getaway is abruptly derailed when he discovers an accidental stowaway on his front porch: Russell (voiced by newcomer Jordan Nagai), an overly enthusiastic 8-year-old "Wilderness Explorer" trying to earn his final merit badge for assisting the elderly.

The dynamic between the reluctant, curmudgeonly senior citizen and the eager, relentless youngster provides the comic engine of the film. Their journey takes them to the jungles of South America, where the narrative picks up steam with the addition of two standout supporting characters:
*   **Kevin:** A giant, chocolate-addicted tropical bird.
*   **Dug:** A golden retriever fitted with a high-tech collar that translates his thoughts into speech (voiced by co-director Bob Peterson), whose line "I have just met you, and I love you" is destined to become an instant classic.

---

### Technical brilliance meets emotional depth

Visually, "Up" is nothing short of extraordinary. The contrast between the bright, pastel balloons floating against a slate-gray cityscape offers some of the most stunning imagery Pixar has ever produced. Furthermore, the film marks Pixar’s first foray into 3D, a format used here with commendable restraint to enhance depth rather than rely on cheap gimmicks.

Underpinning the visual spectacle is a sweeping, nostalgia-infused score by composer Michael Giacchino. His central theme effortlessly shifts from a lighthearted jazz waltz to a mournful swell, acting as the emotional backbone of the narrative.

If the film suffers from any flaw, it is a somewhat conventional third act involving an eccentric explorer (voiced by Christopher Plummer) and a fleet of menacing dogs on airships. While the action set-pieces are thrilling and will undoubtedly keep younger viewers engaged, the film is at its absolute best when focusing on the quieter, human moments between Carl and Russell.

### The Verdict

With "Up," Pixar continues an unmatched hot streak that includes "Ratatouille" and "WALL-E." The film manages to be broad enough to entertain toddlers, funny enough for teenagers, and emotionally resonant enough to deeply move adults.

By reminding us that the greatest adventure in life isn't necessarily found on a map, but in the everyday connections we make with others, "Up" achieves greatness.

**CNN Rating:** ★★★★☆ (Out of four stars)

# Review: Pixar reaches new heights with the sublime, soulful 'Up'

**By Tom Charity** (for CNN)
**May 29, 2009**

**(CNN) —** At this point, it feels almost redundant to ask if Pixar has done it again. Over the past decade and a half, the animation studio has set a standard of artistic and commercial excellence that isn't just unmatched in Hollywood today—it may be unprecedented in film history. Coming off the back of last year’s daring, near-silent masterpiece *WALL-E* and 2007’s sublime *Ratatouille*, the bar for Pixar’s tenth feature could not have been set higher. 

Yet, director Pete Docter (*Monsters, Inc.*) and co-director Bob Peterson haven't just cleared that bar with *Up*; they’ve soared right over it in a brightly colored house lifted by thousands of helium balloons. 

*Up* is a hilarious, visually stunning, and surprisingly profound adventure that proves animated movies aren't just for kids—they are, at their best, simply great cinema. 

### A Masterclass in Visual Storytelling

Before the film sends its elderly protagonist floating into the clouds, *Up* delivers what is undoubtedly the most emotionally devastating and beautiful prologue you will see in a theater this year. 

In a nearly dialogue-free montage lasting less than ten minutes, we witness the life story of Carl Fredricksen and his childhood sweetheart, Ellie. Set to a melancholic, ragtime-infused score by Michael Giacchino, we watch them fall in love, buy a fixer-upper home, dream of traveling to South America’s mysterious Paradise Falls, navigate the heartbreaking reality of infertility, grow old together, and ultimately, face the inevitable quiet sorrow of final separation. 

It is a stunning piece of filmmaking—fearless, mature, and deeply human. By the time the sequence ends with 78-year-old Carl sitting alone in a darkened living room, there won't be a dry eye in the house. It’s a bold move for a "family movie," but it anchors everything that follows in genuine human emotion.

### An Unlikely High-Flying Duo

When the modern world threatens to force Carl out of his home and into a retirement community, the retired balloon salesman takes matters into his own hands. Attaching thousands of colorful, helium-filled balloons to his chimney, he lifts off into the sky, destination: South America. 

There’s just one hitch. 

Stowed away on his porch is Russell, an overly enthusiastic 8-year-old "Wilderness Explorer" missing his "Assisting the Elderly" merit badge. 

The heart of *Up* relies entirely on the dynamic between this mismatched pair. Carl is a grieving, bow-tie-wearing curmudgeon who just wants the world to leave him alone. Russell is a relentless, chubby bundle of energy whose boundless optimism masks his own subtle domestic sadness—a distant father who is never around. 

Their banter is pitch-perfect. As they find themselves dragging Carl’s floating house on foot across the perilous terrain of Paradise Falls, their reluctant grandfather-grandson dynamic evolves with natural warmth. The film never forces the sweetness; it earns it through shared peril, comedic clashes, and the arrival of a few eccentric sidekicks—namely Kevin, a giant, chocolate-loving exotic bird, and Dug, a delightfully dim-witted golden retriever fitted with a collar that translates his thoughts into speech ("I have just met you, and I love you!").

### Perfect Pitch: The Voice Cast

Much of the film’s charm rests on the shoulders of its stellar vocal talent. Pixar has wisely resisted the trend of casting giant pop-culture celebrities for the sake of a marquee name, choosing instead actors who fit the characters seamlessly.

Acting legend Ed Asner was born to play Carl Fredricksen. He brings a rich, gravelly authority to the role, balancing Carl’s crotchety exterior with an underlying softness that keeps the character deeply sympathetic. 

Opposite him, newcomer Jordan Nagai is a revelation as Russell. Rather than hiring a professional child actor with a polished Hollywood delivery, the filmmakers cast Nagai for his natural, unscripted spontaneity. His performance is delightfully authentic—complete with the breathless ramblings real eight-year-olds are prone to.

Rounding out the cast is screen veteran Christopher Plummer, who delivers a sinister, charismatic turn as Charles Muntz, a disgraced 1930s adventurer whose dark obsession with capturing Paradise Falls' rare wildlife mirrors what Carl could become if he lets bitterness consume him.

### 3D Done Right

In a year where Hollywood seems obsessed with forcing 3D glasses onto moviegoers for every summer blockbuster, *Up* arrives as a masterclass in how to use the technology thoughtfully. 

As Pixar’s first foray into Disney Digital 3D, the film mercifully avoids cheap, gimmicky trickery. You won't find objects constantly poking out of the screen just to startle you. Instead, Docter and his team use the third dimension to create staggering cinematic spatial depth. 

When Carl’s house lifts above the grey, concrete skyline of the city into the vast blue yonder, the sense of scale is breathtaking. Later, when the characters navigate treacherous, misty cliffs thousands of feet above the jungle floor, the 3D enhances the dizzying vertigo and sense of adventure. It draws you *into* the story rather than pulling you out of it.

### The Verdict

*Up* is a rare treasure: a wildly inventive action-adventure that doubles as a delicate meditation on grief, aging, and what it truly means to live a life of adventure. It proves that the greatest journey isn't necessarily found in far-off, uncharted lands, but in the everyday moments we share with the people we love.

Pixar hasn’t just delivered the best movie of the summer—they’ve delivered an instant classic.

**Gravity and Grace: How Pixar’s *Up* Balances Devastating Grief with High-Flying Absurdity**

When Pixar’s *Up* premiered in 2009, it pulled off one of the most audacious narrative feats in modern animated cinema. Directed by Pete Docter and Bob Peterson, the film asks its audience to hold two radically different movie experiences in their heads simultaneously: a devastating, naturalistic meditation on aging and spousal loss, and a vibrant, pulp-adventure romp featuring a floating house, a relentless boy scout, a colorful exotic bird, and a pack of talking dogs. That *Up* not only survives this jarring tonal pivot but soars because of it is a testament to Pixar’s masterclass in thematic storytelling.

The film’s legendary prologue—a four-minute, mostly dialogue-free montage set to Michael Giacchino’s Oscar-winning score—is arguably the finest sequence Pixar has ever produced. We witness the life of Carl and Ellie Fredricksen, from childhood sweethearts to a devoted married couple, navigating the quiet joys and crushing heartbreak of ordinary life. We see their dreams deferred, a miscarried pregnancy, the slow decay of youth, and ultimately, Ellie’s death, leaving an elderly Carl alone in a home surrounded by corporate encroachment. It is a masterpiece of pathos, grounding the viewer in visceral human pain. 

By all rights, what follows should cause severe narrative whiplash. Driven by a desire to fulfill a lifelong promise to his late wife, Carl attaches thousands of helium balloons to his chimney and takes flight toward South America’s Paradise Falls. Shortly after takeoff, the film shifts gears entirely, morphing from a somber drama into a colorful, fast-paced odd-couple comedy.

The catalyst for this transition is Russell, an overly enthusiastic, father-starved "Wilderness Explorer" who inadvertently stowaways on Carl’s porch. Russell’s earnest, chatterbox energy breaks Carl’s melancholic silence, forcing the grumpy widower out of his mournful shell. Upon landing in the Venezuelan jungle, the absurdities multiply exponential. Enter Kevin, a 13-foot tall, chocolate-obsessed, neon-feathered bird, and Dug, a dopey Golden Retriever equipped with a translator collar that broadcasts his every thought ("I have just met you, and I love you!"). 

On paper, transitioning from the quiet tragedy of infertility and widowhood to a pack of villainous Dobermans and Alpha-dogs communicating via electronic voices should feel like two entirely different scripts clumsily stitched together. Yet, *Up* succeeds because it uses its high-concept adventure as a physical metaphor for Carl’s psychological state.

The floating house itself is the ultimate visual symbol of grief. Carl isn't just dragging a building across the South American landscape; he is literally hauling the crushing weight of his past, refusing to let go of Ellie’s memory. The chaotic, living companions he meets along the way—Russell, Kevin, and Dug—represent the unpredictable, messy reality of the present. The laugh-out-loud comedy generated by Dug’s dog-logic ("Squirrel!") and Russell’s ineptitude isn't just superficial kid-bait; it serves as a therapeutic counterweight to Carl’s grief. They are pulling him back toward life, whether he wants it or not.

If the film has a flaw, it lies in its third act, where the demands of a traditional Disney/Pixar climax slightly undercut its nuanced themes. The introduction of Charles Muntz—Carl’s childhood hero turned crazed, dog-army-commanding aviator—feels a bit forced. The climax features dog fights in vintage biplanes and sword fights with walking canes. While wildly entertaining and impeccably animated, it briefly threatens to transform a deeply personal story about letting go into a standard action spectacle.

However, Docter and Peterson bring the emotional plane down for a perfect landing. The film’s true climax isn't Muntz’s defeat, but the moment Carl opens Ellie’s "Adventure Book" and discovers her final message: *"Thanks for the adventure—now go have a new one."* It is here that the ridiculous elements—the talking dogs, the wilderness badges, the colorful bird—cohere. Ellie's adventure wasn't the destination of Paradise Falls; it was the life they shared, and the new, unconventional family Carl has blundered into.

*Up* remains a triumph of emotional range. It proves that animation can tackle the heaviest elements of the human experience—grief, aging, and mortality—without losing the sense of child-like wonder that makes the medium special. By anchoring its flying house and talking dogs in genuine human sorrow, Pixar created a film that doesn't just entertain; it lifts the spirit.
